assessment: Full assembly plausibly checks physical fit before shipping, and repeated three-compartment orders approach the time target (D2-O6). Nevertheless, combined timing cannot locate the delay (D2-O2), customer reports do not establish every packing error (D2-O3), and three unpackers needed short-partition guidance (D2-O4). Mixed batches contain the longest orders, but layout complexity confounds a switching explanation. The concrete limiting observation is overlapping widths among first-attempt and retried partitions (D2-O5): width alone does not explain insertion difficulty. These stipulated observations support hypotheses, not demonstrated remedies or pilot success.

openings.claim: Does switching between layouts increase selection/checking time independently of compartment count?
openings.delta: Separates a workflow explanation for mixed-batch delays from the inherent work of larger layouts.
openings.prediction: A switching effect would increase selection/checking time for the same layout after a different layout; inherent complexity would instead track compartment count across both sequences.
openings.probe: Use reusable sample parts for both workers to complete matched repeated-layout and alternating-layout sequences, counterbalancing sequence order and matching exterior color. Record selection, insertion, checking and packing separately, and independently audit contents. Include all three compartment counts. Limit this exploratory trial to existing resources and time compatible with the fixed delivery date.
assumptions: Reusable samples permit matched trials within spare-board and time limits.
Practice and worker differences can be recorded; small trials cannot establish pilot success.

openings.claim: An order-specific diagram identifying each short partition's destination may improve unaided arrangement when the supplied parts are correct.
openings.delta: Tests whether ambiguity in the three-layout diagram contributes to difficulty, separately from missing or incorrect components.
openings.prediction: With independently verified identical kits, customers receiving the order-specific diagram should make fewer short-partition placement errors and requests for help than customers receiving the current diagram.
openings.probe: Randomly assign the ten willing participants to the current or order-specific diagram, balancing layouts as practicable. Observe ordered-layout completion and short-partition errors without coaching. Check incremental printing cost and preparation time before adoption; preserve supplied components, reversible joints, colors, counts and delivery date.
assumptions: Diagram production fits the 500 initial and 0.40 recurring cost ceilings.
Correct-kit difficulty is partly informational rather than entirely physical.
Ten participants provide exploratory discrimination, not validation of the 90% customer target.
